item.question: Try another example: 80 and 63. 80 = 40 × 2 = 20 × 4 = 10 × 8 = 16 × 5 = ??? and 63 = 9 × 7 = 3 × 21 = ??? Taking 80 = 16 × 5 and 63 = 9 × 7 there are no common factors. Can we conclude that 80 and 63 are co-prime?
steps: Factorisations shown are only some of the ways
Anshu's mistake shows absence of a common factor in chosen factorisations proves nothing
item.answer: No. Looking at one chosen factorisation of each number cannot show they are co-prime, because there may be other ways to factorise (other factors) that we have not seen. We need a more systematic approach.
item.text:

1. Factorisations shown are only some of the ways
2. Anshu's mistake shows absence of a common factor in chosen factorisations proves nothing
Answer: No. Looking at one chosen factorisation of each number cannot show they are co-prime, because there may be other ways to factorise (other factors) that we have not seen. We need a more systematic approach.

item.question: Using this diagram, can you explain why 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, no matter which way you multiply 2, 3, and 5?
steps: The diagram is a cuboid made of unit cubes with 3 cubes along the front width, 2 along the height and 5 along the depth, so it has 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cubes. Counting the same cubes layer by layer in any direction gives the same total, so the order of multiplication does not change the product. (Commutativity and associativity of multiplication, to be studied in a later class.)

item.question: Teacher asks: Are 56 and 63 co-prime? Anshu writes 56 = 14 × 4 and 63 = 21 × 3 and says there are no common factors, so they are co-prime. Guna writes 56 = 7 × 8 and 63 = 9 × 7 and says 7 is a common factor, so they are not co-prime. Guna is right. But where did Anshu go wrong?
steps_tex: $56 = 14 \times 4$ gives only some factors of $56$ ($14$ and $4$)
item.answer_tex: Writing $56 = 14 \times 4$ only shows that $14$ and $4$ are factors of $56$; it does not list all factors of $56$ (same for $63$). Anshu missed the common factor $7$ because one factorisation does not reveal every factor.

So 56 and 63 are not co-prime

item.question: 80 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 and 63 = 3 × 3 × 7. There are no common prime factors. Can we conclude that they are co-prime? Suppose they have a common factor that is composite. Would the prime factors of this composite common factor appear in the prime factorisation of 80 and 63?
steps: Yes. A composite common factor would be a product of primes that divide both numbers, so its prime factors would appear in both prime factorisations. Since there are no common prime factors, there is no common factor other than 1, so 80 and 63 are co-prime. If there are no common prime factors, the two numbers are co-prime.

item.question: We say that 48 is divisible by 12 because when we divide 48 by 12, the remainder is zero. How can we check if one number is divisible by another without carrying out long division?
steps: Use prime factorisations: a number is divisible by another if the prime factorisation of the second number is included in the prime factorisation of the first (see the Examples 168 by 12, 75 by 21, 42 by 12). e.g. 48 = 2×2×2×2×3 includes 12 = 2×2×3.
